name: revenue_recognition_5step_model
text: ASC 606 recognizes revenue from contracts with customers under a five-step model: (1) identify the contract with the customer; (2) identify the performance obligations in the contract; (3) determine the transaction price; (4) allocate the transaction price to the performance obligations; and (5) recognize revenue as (or when) each performance obligation is satisfied. Because each performance obligation is accounted for separately, identifying the obligations and allocating the transaction price among them drives the recognition pattern and timing.

name: contract_identification
text: A contract with a customer is within the scope of the standard only when all of the following are met: the parties have approved the contract and are committed to perform their obligations; each party's rights regarding the goods or services are identifiable; the payment terms are identifiable; the contract has commercial substance; and it is probable the entity will collect substantially all of the consideration to which it is entitled. Where payment terms are not yet established, the arrangement is terminable by either party at will without compensation, or collectibility is not probable, the existence of a valid contract is in doubt and revenue is not recognized until the criteria are satisfied.

name: distinct_test
text: A good or service is a distinct performance obligation when both criteria are met: (a) the customer can benefit from the good or service on its own or together with other resources readily available to the customer (capable of being distinct); and (b) the entity's promise to transfer it is separately identifiable from other promises in the contract (distinct within the context of the contract). If a promised good or service is not distinct, it is combined with other promised goods or services until a distinct bundle is identified. A good or service that is capable of being distinct may still fail criterion (b) because, in the context of the specific contract, it is not separately identifiable from the other promises.

name: separately_identifiable_factors
text: In evaluating whether a promise is separately identifiable, the objective is to determine whether the entity is transferring each good or service individually or, instead, a combined item to which the individual goods or services are inputs. Factors indicating that two or more promises are not separately identifiable include: the entity provides a significant service of integrating the goods or services into a combined output; one or more of the goods or services significantly modifies or customizes another; or the goods or services are highly interdependent or highly interrelated. Implementation, configuration, data-migration, or setup activities that an entity must complete before the customer can access or operate the underlying service typically indicate the promises are not separately identifiable and are therefore combined into a single performance obligation.

name: series_of_services
text: A series of distinct goods or services that are substantially the same and have the same pattern of transfer to the customer is accounted for as a single performance obligation. This applies when each distinct increment is satisfied over time and the same method would be used to measure progress toward satisfaction. A subscription that provides continuous access to a hosted application over the contract period is the typical example: it is treated as a single performance obligation satisfied over time, rather than as a series of separately accounted-for daily or monthly promises.

name: over_time_recognition
text: An entity recognizes revenue over time if any one of the following criteria is met: (a) the customer simultaneously receives and consumes the benefits provided as the entity performs; (b) the entity's performance creates or enhances an asset the customer controls as it is created or enhanced; or (c) the entity's performance does not create an asset with an alternative use to the entity, and the entity has an enforceable right to payment for performance completed to date. Software-as-a-service arrangements generally meet criterion (a), because the customer continuously receives and consumes the benefit of access throughout the term; subscription revenue is therefore recognized over the service period rather than at a point in time.

name: measuring_progress_methods
text: For a performance obligation satisfied over time, the entity selects a single method to measure progress toward complete satisfaction. Output methods recognize revenue based on the value of goods or services transferred to date (for a stand-ready obligation such as access to a platform, a time-based measure is often appropriate, resulting in straight-line recognition). Input methods recognize revenue based on the entity's efforts or inputs (for example, labor hours or costs incurred) and are appropriate where effort, rather than the passage of time, faithfully depicts the transfer of control — such as a consulting or professional-services engagement in which effort is concentrated unevenly across the period.

name: variable_consideration
text: If the consideration in a contract includes a variable amount — arising from usage- or volume-based fees, rebates, refunds, credits, price concessions, performance bonuses, penalties, or similar items — the entity estimates the amount to which it expects to be entitled. The estimate is made using either the expected value (the sum of probability-weighted amounts, appropriate when there is a large number of possible outcomes) or the most likely amount (appropriate when the contract has only a few possible outcomes), whichever better predicts the consideration. Consumption- or usage-based fees in a subscription represent variable consideration because the total depends on the customer's actual usage.

name: constraint_variable_consideration
text: Variable consideration is included in the transaction price only to the extent it is highly probable that a significant reversal of cumulative revenue recognized will not occur when the uncertainty associated with the variable consideration is subsequently resolved. Factors that increase the likelihood of a significant reversal — and therefore warrant constraining the estimate — include consideration that is highly susceptible to factors outside the entity's influence, uncertainty not expected to resolve for a long period, limited relevant experience, broad ranges of possible amounts, or highly variable (for example, seasonal) usage.

name: right_to_invoice_expedient
text: As a practical expedient, if an entity has a right to consideration from a customer in an amount that corresponds directly with the value to the customer of the entity's performance completed to date (for example, a fixed amount for each unit of service delivered), the entity may recognize revenue in the amount to which it has a right to invoice. This permits recognition of usage-based amounts as the related usage occurs, without estimating the total variable consideration over the remaining term.

name: usage_based_royalty
topic: Step 3 — sales- or usage-based royalty exception
text: For a license of intellectual property where the consideration is a sales- or usage-based royalty, the entity recognizes revenue at the later of when the subsequent sale or usage occurs, or when the performance obligation to which the royalty has been allocated has been satisfied (in whole or in part). This royalty constraint is an exception to the general variable-consideration guidance and applies specifically because the variable amount is consideration for a license of the entity's intellectual property rather than for ordinary service usage.

name: allocate_by_ssp
topic: Step 4 — allocation based on standalone selling price
text: When a contract has more than one performance obligation, the entity allocates the transaction price to each performance obligation in proportion to the standalone selling prices of the underlying goods or services. The standalone selling price is the price at which an entity would sell a promised good or service separately to a customer. The best evidence of standalone selling price is the observable price of the good or service when the entity sells it separately in similar circumstances and to similar customers.

name: estimating_ssp
text: If a standalone selling price is not directly observable, the entity estimates it using an approach that maximizes the use of observable inputs, such as: an adjusted market assessment approach (estimating the price customers would be willing to pay); an expected-cost-plus-a-margin approach; or a residual approach. Under the residual approach the entity estimates the standalone selling price as the total transaction price less the observable standalone selling prices of the other goods or services in the contract; it is appropriate only where the selling price is highly variable or uncertain (for example, not yet established or sold to a broad range of customers at widely varying prices).

name: allocating_a_discount
text: A contract contains a discount when the sum of the standalone selling prices of the promised goods or services exceeds the total consideration. A discount is generally allocated proportionately to all performance obligations on the basis of their relative standalone selling prices. A discount is allocated to one or more, but not all, performance obligations only when the entity has observable evidence that the discount relates to those specific obligations — namely, the entity regularly sells each good or service on a standalone basis, regularly sells a bundle of some of those goods or services at a discount, and the discount attributable to that bundle is substantially the same as the discount in the contract.

name: material_right
text: An option granting the customer the right to acquire additional goods or services free or at a discount gives rise to a separate performance obligation if it provides a material right — that is, a right the customer would not receive without entering into the contract, such as a discount incremental to the range of discounts typically given to that class of customer. When a material right exists (for example, a significantly discounted renewal option, or a free or reduced-price future add-on), the entity allocates a portion of the transaction price to it and recognizes that amount when the future goods or services are transferred or when the option expires.

name: nonrefundable_upfront_fees
text: A nonrefundable upfront fee (for example, an activation, setup, or initiation fee) is assessed to determine whether it relates to the transfer of a promised good or service. If the upfront fee does not relate to a distinct good or service, it is an advance payment for future goods or services and is recognized as revenue when those future goods or services are provided. Where the fee, combined with the customer's option to renew without paying it again, effectively provides a material right with respect to future contract periods, a portion of the fee is allocated to that right.

name: contract_liability_and_asset
text: Differences in the timing of billing and performance are presented as contract balances. When a customer pays consideration, or an amount of consideration is due, before the entity transfers the related goods or services, the entity recognizes a contract liability (commonly described as deferred revenue), which is recognized as revenue as performance occurs. When the entity has transferred goods or services but its right to consideration is conditional on something other than the passage of time, it recognizes a contract asset rather than a receivable; a receivable is recognized when the right to consideration is unconditional.

name: contract_modifications
text: A contract modification is a change in the scope or price (or both) of a contract approved by the parties. A modification is accounted for as a separate contract if it adds distinct goods or services priced at their standalone selling prices. If it is not a separate contract, the entity accounts for the modification prospectively (allocating the remaining consideration to the remaining performance obligations) when the remaining goods or services are distinct, or on a cumulative catch-up basis when they are not distinct and form part of a single performance obligation partially satisfied. Determining the appropriate treatment requires the added scope and the change in price.
